screens.title: Context Managers and the with Statement
screens.narratorSegment: Resource leaks happen when acquired resources are not released: files stay open, locks remain locked, or temporary directories stick around. In Python, the with statement paired with context managers gives you a clear, reliable pattern: acquire a resource, run code that uses it, and always run cleanup when the block exits. You will learn the protocol that makes an object a context manager, how to implement it with enter and exit, and a concise alternative with contextlib's @contextmanager. We will ground ideas with concrete examples: opening files, a custom database connection class, and a temporary-directory manager. Finally, we examine common mistakes so you can avoid leaks and subtle exception handling errors. By the end, you'll be able to pick the right approach for most resource management needs and write context managers that behave correctly even when exceptions happen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Context Managers
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Master resource safety with context managers

Learn how the with statement ensures setup and teardown run reliably for files, locks, sockets, and temporary resources. We'll show class-based and generator-based patterns and practical pitfalls to avoid.

Real problem: a file left open
If an error interrupts your code, explicit close calls may never run. with guarantees cleanup.
Two ways to build managers
Use class-based __enter__/__exit__ for full control or @contextmanager for concise generators.
Explore Key Topics
Files
with open(...) auto-closes file handles even on error.
Custom Classes
Implement __enter__ and __exit__ to control acquisition and cleanup.
contextlib
@contextmanager turns a generator into a context manager with a yield point.
Problem → with Statement → Result
Problem
A file is opened and an error occurs before close is called, leaving system handles open.
with Example
with open("my_file.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Hello, Cohortia!
")
# f.close() is automatic
Result
Cleanup runs whether the block completes or raises an exception, preventing leaks and improving reliability.

screens.title: What a context manager is
screens.narratorSegment: A context manager defines a runtime context that performs setup when you enter a block and teardown when you exit it. That setup-teardown pair is often described as acquire-release. The context manager protocol requires two methods: enter and exit. enter performs setup work and typically returns the resource used inside the block. exit receives information about any exception that occurred in the block: the exception type, value, and traceback. It performs cleanup, and by returning True it can suppress the exception so it does not propagate. A common misconception is that with magically prevents exceptions; it does not. Instead, it guarantees that cleanup runs. For example, opening a file returns a context manager whose enter returns a file object and whose exit closes it automatically. Understanding that separation of responsibilities—acquire in enter, release in exit—helps you design predictable resource-handling code and avoid leaks. Can you name a resource in your own projects that would benefit from this pattern? What a context manager is means context managers guarantee setup and teardown around a code block; __enter__ acquires, __exit__ releases and sees exceptions.. In practical terms, the acquire-release pattern formalized for safe resource handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept What a context manager is
Definition

Context manager protocol

Implement two methods to support with: __enter__ for setup and __exit__ for teardown. __exit__ gets exception details and can suppress exceptions by returning True.

__enter__
Return a resource and perform acquisition. Example: the opened file object.
__exit__
Run cleanup and examine exception info. Returning True suppresses the exception.
Key Takeaway

The with statement does not hide errors; it guarantees cleanup regardless of errors.

Analogy: door open / door close

Think of __enter__ as opening a door to a controlled environment, and __exit__ as closing it and cleaning up the room. Even if smoke is inside, you still close the door on the way out.

Concrete example
with open("my_file.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Hello, Cohortia!
")
# File is closed automatically on block exit
Common misconception
Context managers suppress exceptions by default. Clarification: they may suppress exceptions only if __exit__ explicitly returns True; otherwise exceptions propagate after cleanup.

screens.title: What with guarantees
screens.narratorSegment: The with statement follows a clear three-step process. First, Python evaluates the context expression and calls enter on the returned context manager; this performs acquisition or setup and often returns the resource that the block will use. Second, Python executes the block body using the bound resource from the as clause if present. Third, when the block completes or an exception occurs, Python calls exit with three arguments describing the exception if one happened: the exception type, value, and traceback. The exit method performs cleanup actions such as closing files or releasing locks. If exit returns True, Python treats the exception as handled and does not re-raise it; if it returns False or None, the exception continues to propagate after cleanup. A common error is forgetting to handle exceptions inside exit when you intend to suppress them. Always ensure cleanup happens in exit regardless of exceptions, and explicitly decide whether suppression is desired. Try tracing these three steps in a short snippet and intentionally raise an error inside the with block to see cleanup behavior. What with guarantees means with calls __enter__, runs the block, then calls __exit__ with exception info — cleanup always executes.. In practical terms, step-by-step: enter, run, exit (even on error). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Class-based context managers
screens.narratorSegment: Class-based context managers give you explicit control over resource lifecycle. You typically initialize the helper in init, perform acquisition in enter, and put cleanup in exit. enter often returns the resource object that code inside the with block will use. exit accepts three parameters describing any exception that occurred inside the block. Inside exit you should release or close resources and optionally inspect the exception to respond or suppress it. Returning False or None indicates the exception should propagate after cleanup; returning True suppresses it. A common use case is a custom database connection: enter sets up the connection and returns a usable connection object, and exit commits or rolls back and closes the connection. A typical mistake is putting expensive acquisition logic in init and not in enter; prefer acquiring in enter so object construction does not perform the side effects before entering the with block. Designing class-based managers is best when you need fine-grained control over both setup and teardown semantics. Class-based context managers means use __enter__ for acquiring and returning the resource, __exit__ for cleanup and optional exception handling.. In practical terms, implementing __enter__ and __exit__ for full control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Class-based

Example: DatabaseConnection

class DatabaseConnection:
    def __init__(self, db_name):
        self.db_name = db_name
        self.connection = None

    def __enter__(self):
        print(f"Connecting to database: {self.db_name}...")
        self.connection = f"Connection object for {self.db_name}"
        return self.connection

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        if exc_type:
            print(f"An error occurred: {exc_val}")
        print(f"Closing connection to database: {self.db_name}...")
        self.connection = None
        return False

Notes and best practices

  • Do acquisition in __enter__ to avoid side effects at construction time.
  • Use __exit__ to always release, even when exceptions occur.
  • Carefully decide whether to suppress exceptions; prefer explicit returns.
Pro tip
Log context transitions in __enter__ and __exit__ to help debug resource leaks during development.

screens.title: Generator-based managers with @contextmanager
screens.narratorSegment: For simpler setup-teardown logic, contextlib's @contextmanager decorator lets you write a generator function that becomes a context manager. Code before the yield acts like enter: it runs at the start and prepares the resource. The value yielded is what the with statement binds to the as name. Code after yield is the teardown and runs when the block exits; if an exception occurs inside the with block, it is re-raised at the yield point inside the generator, so you can catch it there. Use try/finally around yield to ensure cleanup always runs. This approach is more concise and readable for many common cases. A common mistake is forgetting to yield a value when an as clause is expected, which will cause the bound variable to be None or raise an error. Additionally, be explicit about exception handling inside the generator: decide whether to handle or re-raise. Generator-based managers are excellent for simple resource wrappers like temporary directories or timing contexts where you do not need the full lifecycle control of a class. Generator-based managers with @contextmanager means use @contextmanager and yield; pre-yield is enter, post-yield is exit, and exceptions are re-raised at the yield point.. In practical terms, a concise alternative using yield for setup and teardown. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use @contextmanager and yield; pre-yield is enter, post-yield is exit, and exceptions are re-raised at the yield point.

content.html:
Core Concept
contextlib

@contextmanager example

from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def db_connection_generator(db_name):
    conn = None
    try:
        print(f"Connecting to database: {db_name}...")
        conn = f"Connection object for {db_name}"
        yield conn
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"An error occurred in the with block: {e}")
    finally:
        if conn:
            print(f"Closing connection to database: {db_name}...")
            conn = None

When to choose this

  • Use for short setup/teardown that maps naturally to a single yield point.
  • Avoid for managers needing complex state between enter and exit that benefits from explicit methods.
  • Always wrap yield in try/finally to guarantee teardown.
Misconception
@contextmanager is just syntactic sugar. It is sugar, but it also changes how exceptions are propagated because they re-enter the generator at yield.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Temporary Directory
Starter requirements
  • Create a directory with tempfile.mkdtemp()
  • Return the path from __enter__ or yield it from the generator
  • Remove the directory in __exit__ or finally using shutil.rmtree()
  • Handle missing directory checks to avoid errors during cleanup
Starter code (template)
import tempfile
import shutil
import os
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def temporary_directory_generator():
    temp_dir_path = None
    try:
        temp_dir_path = tempfile.mkdtemp()
        print(f"DEBUG: Created temporary directory: {temp_dir_path}")
        yield temp_dir_path
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"An error occurred within the temporary directory block: {e}")
    finally:
        if temp_dir_path and os.path.exists(temp_dir_path):
            print(f"DEBUG: Removing temporary directory: {temp_dir_path}")
            shutil.rmtree(temp_dir_path)
Test idea
Inside the with block create a file then raise an error; after the block assert the directory path does not exist.

screens.title: Class-based vs @contextmanager

screens.title: Pitfalls and exception handling
screens.narratorSegment: There are several practical pitfalls to watch for. First, failing to perform cleanup inside exit or a finally block means resources remain held when exceptions occur. Second, returning True from exit without careful consideration can hide bugs; only suppress exceptions when you have explicitly handled them. Third, performing expensive acquisition in init rather than enter can cause side effects before the with block starts. Fourth, generator-based managers must yield a value when an as clause is used; forgetting the yield or yielding the wrong object leads to confusing None values or attribute errors. Finally, assume that the cleanup itself can fail; guard against that by checking existence before removal and catching exceptions inside teardown logging them rather than letting cleanup throw and mask the original error. Testing both normal and exceptional flows helps catch these mistakes early. Build simple unit tests that raise exceptions inside the with block to confirm cleanup always runs. Error handling
Missing cleanup

screens.title: When to use context managers
screens.narratorSegment: Context managers are useful wherever resources must be released reliably. Common scenarios include file input and output, where file handles must be closed; threading locks, which must be released to avoid deadlock; network sockets, which should be closed to free ports; temporary directories and files that must be removed; and database connections that must be closed or returned to a pool. They are also helpful for temporarily changing state, such as switching directories or altering logging configuration, where you want to restore previous state on exit. A good rule is: when you have paired actions—acquire and release—consider a context manager. Using with improves readability and reduces boilerplate try/finally blocks. Additionally, many standard library objects already implement the protocol, so prefer using their context manager behavior rather than reimplementing manual acquisition and release. Finally, write tests that intentionally raise exceptions inside with blocks to ensure your context managers reliably perform teardown. Resource leaks happen when acquired resources are not released: files stay open, locks remain locked, or temporary directories stick around. In Python, the with statement paired with context managers gives you a clear, reliable pattern: acquire a resource, run code that uses it, and always run cleanup when the block exits. You will learn the protocol that makes an object a context manager, how to implement it with enter and exit, and a concise alternative with contextlib's @contextmanager. We will ground ideas with concrete examples: opening files, a custom database connection class, and a temporary-directory manager. Finally, we examine common mistakes so you can avoid leaks and subtle exception handling errors. By the end, you'll be able to pick the right approach for most resource management needs and write context managers that behave correctly even when exceptions happen.

In this lesson you will learn four practical skills that make your Python code safer and easier to read. First, you will explain what context managers and the with statement are and why they matter for resource reliability. Second, you'll practice using with to manage files and locks so cleanup happens automatically. Third, you'll implement class-based context managers by writing enter and exit methods so you can control setup and teardown precisely. Fourth, you'll create concise context managers with contextlib and the @contextmanager decorator for simpler cases. Each objective links to a real scenario: files left open, locks that cause deadlocks, connections that must close, and temporary directories that must be removed. We'll also include a verified competency milestone that helps you confirm correct behavior under normal and error paths. Understanding these skills prevents common bugs and reduces the cognitive load of resource cleanup, which is essential when building robust scripts and services.

This screen shows how you will practice and verify the skills. For explaining context managers, you'll read an example where a file is not closed and describe why with fixes it. For using with in code, you'll refactor a manual acquire/release pattern to use with and write a small test that raises an exception to confirm cleanup still runs. For class-based managers, you'll implement enter to return the resource and exit to clean up and log exceptions; your test should assert that resources are set to None after exit. For generator-based managers with @contextmanager, you'll use a try/finally around yield so cleanup always runs, and verify temporary directories are removed after both normal and exceptional exits. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can prove your code handles both success and error paths.

A context manager defines a runtime context that performs setup when you enter a block and teardown when you exit it. That setup-teardown pair is often described as acquire-release. The context manager protocol requires two methods: enter and exit. enter performs setup work and typically returns the resource used inside the block. exit receives information about any exception that occurred in the block: the exception type, value, and traceback. It performs cleanup, and by returning True it can suppress the exception so it does not propagate. A common misconception is that with magically prevents exceptions; it does not. Instead, it guarantees that cleanup runs. For example, opening a file returns a context manager whose enter returns a file object and whose exit closes it automatically. Understanding that separation of responsibilities—acquire in enter, release in exit—helps you design predictable resource-handling code and avoid leaks. The with statement follows a clear three-step process. First, Python evaluates the context expression and calls enter on the returned context manager; this performs acquisition or setup and often returns the resource that the block will use. Second, Python executes the block body using the bound resource from the as clause if present. Third, when the block completes or an exception occurs, Python calls exit with three arguments describing the exception if one happened: the exception type, value, and traceback. The exit method performs cleanup actions such as closing files or releasing locks. If exit returns True, Python treats the exception as handled and does not re-raise it; if it returns False or None, the exception continues to propagate after cleanup. A common error is forgetting to handle exceptions inside exit when you intend to suppress them.
